name: Factory Bloom
origin: The automotive manufacturing corridor of Michigan's lower peninsula contains, embedded in the concrete floors of its abandoned assembly plants, decades of compacted industrial byproduct: cutting fluids, press lubricants, hydraulic compounds, and the specific polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons generated by continuous heavy manufacturing across nearly a century of operation. The Factory Bloom is what grew out of it when the last plants went dark and the buildings stopped being maintained. It is not a plant in any traditional sense — it photosynthesizes through modified chlorophyll analogs that process wavelengths of light that fall outside the visible spectrum, which is why the first observers did not understand what they were looking at. It looked like rust. Then it looked like rust that was moving. Then it was too large to mistake for anything.
substrate: Photosynthetic-industrial hybrid organism. The metabolic substrate is the industrial compound layer in the concrete floors of its host structures. It does not consume the concrete — it consumes the chemical deposits within and beneath it, producing orange-gold crystalline fruiting bodies as metabolic byproduct. These fruiting bodies are its most visible feature: dense, branching crystalline structures that rise from floor and wall surfaces at heights of up to two meters in mature growth zones, orange-gold in ambient light, bioluminescent in darkness, pulsing at an extremely slow rhythm — one full cycle per twenty to forty minutes — that is only perceptible to observation over extended periods.
territory: The interior spaces of large abandoned industrial structures with specific floor chemistry: automotive plants, stamping facilities, machine shops, and heavy manufacturing buildings. The chemical compound that feeds it is specific enough that it does not grow in warehouses, office buildings, or light industrial facilities. It requires the floor chemistry of heavy manufacturing, which limits its range to a specific geographic and industrial corridor through Michigan, Indiana, and northeastern Ohio.
physical_description: At a distance, inside an old assembly plant, Factory Bloom reads as a landscape. The floor has been transformed into a low forest of crystalline growth, orange-gold structures rising from a base layer of flat orange mat that covers every exposed surface of the floor and lower walls. The ceiling is often clear — the organism does not grow upward past the structural limit it has established, which varies by facility but typically stops at approximately three meters. The fruiting bodies are fragile-looking but not fragile — they flex rather than shatter under moderate force, with a quality that researchers have compared to dense mineral foam. In darkness, the bioluminescence is visible from outside the building through any gap in the exterior — a faint amber glow that has given rise to the local name 'the Orange Problem' among people in adjacent areas who see it through windows at night.
behavioral_profile: The organism does not move in any conventional sense. It grows — slowly, predictably, outward from established zones at a rate of approximately one to three meters per year depending on substrate richness. It does not respond to the presence of animals or humans in any documented way — there is no defensive behavior, no predatory behavior, no apparent awareness of biological visitors. It is, as far as anyone can determine, simply growing: consuming the chemical legacy of a century of manufacturing and converting it into light and crystal. The bioluminescence increases measurably in the presence of rainfall and humidity changes, suggesting a reproductive or spore-distribution function, but no mechanism for dispersal has been confirmed. It has not spread to new structures in thirty years of observation. The existing colonies are larger than they were, but no new establishment sites have been confirmed.
threat_level: Minimal physical threat. The crystal structures are not toxic to touch. The metabolic output is not hazardous in the concentrations present in an inhabited building — the main byproduct is a specific ester compound that is detectable by smell (a sweet, slightly chemical odor, similar to industrial cleaner at very low concentration) and which produces mild vasodilation with extended exposure. Workers who spent extended periods in early colonized buildings before the organism was identified reported persistent headaches, slight euphoria, and elevated heart rate consistent with mild vasodilator exposure. At no point has a fatal or serious injury been attributed to Factory Bloom. The structural danger is the standard hazard of the decaying buildings it inhabits, not the organism itself.
human_remnants: The assembly line infrastructure of its host buildings has been incorporated into the bloom's architecture in ways that are difficult to distinguish from deliberate arrangement. Conveyor segments, press housing, tooling racks, and vehicle assembly fixtures all show varying degrees of colonization — the crystal growth follows the lines of the machinery with a fidelity that looks purposeful. The orbital of a stamping press becomes the nucleus of a bloom cluster. A fifty-meter body assembly line becomes a corridor of crystalline arches. The overhead crane rails in a body shop, colonized along their full length, glow amber in the dark like the memory of the operation that once ran beneath them.
known_locations: Former River Rouge Complex, Dearborn MI — the largest known bloom, estimated 40% floor coverage across multiple buildings
Packard Plant remnants, Detroit MI — confirmed secondary colony
Inland Steel facility, East Chicago IN — westernmost confirmed colony
Multiple smaller stamping plants in the Michigan-Ohio-Indiana triangle — at least twelve confirmed sites
glmz_migration_risk: Very low. The organism requires a specific substrate chemistry that does not exist in GLMZ's infrastructure. Its growth rate is slow and its dispersal mechanism unconfirmed. The theoretical concern is GLMZ's outer industrial zones — old manufacturing blocks in the western approaches — but no Factory Bloom has been detected east of the Indiana-Ohio border in any quantity sufficient for establishment. The organism is being actively studied by at least two GLMZ-adjacent corponations for the bioluminescence mechanism and the crystalline byproduct, which has industrial applications.
story_hooks: A corponation's materials science division wants a quantity of mature Factory Bloom crystal — enough to analyze the bioluminescence mechanism. The bloom is on-site and accessible, but the old plant it inhabits is claimed by two separate parties, neither of whom has a clear title to land in the depopulated zone, and both of whom want payment for access.

Someone is living in a Factory Bloom plant. Not squatting — living. A permanent residence established among the crystal structures, with food stores and sleeping arrangements and what appears to be a garden growing in the ambient bioluminescence. The runner is sent to make contact on behalf of a party interested in the inhabitant's knowledge of the organism. Whether the inhabitant wants to be found is a different question.

The bloom in one plant has started growing upward. It was not doing this a month ago. Something about the substrate or light conditions has changed and the growth pattern is different — taller structures, faster expansion, and a new fruiting body shape that no one has documented before. The researchers who study the organism want someone to go in and collect samples before the structural changes make the building dangerous.
